directAnswer: To use a linked list, you need to define a node structure and implement methods for adding, removing, and traversing nodes.
summary: Linked lists are dynamic data structures that allow for efficient insertion and deletion of elements.

sections.heading: Defining the Node Structure
sections.body: A linked list consists of nodes, where each node contains data and a reference to the next node. In languages like Python, you can define a node as a class with attributes for data and the next node.

sections.heading: Basic Operations
sections.body: Key operations include adding a node (to the front, back, or at a specific position), removing a node, and traversing the list to access elements.

sections.heading: Implementation Examples

steps.title: Define the Node Class
steps.detail: Create a class for the node that includes data and a pointer to the next node.

steps.title: Create the Linked List Class
steps.detail: Define a class for the linked list that initializes the head and includes methods for adding and removing nodes.

steps.title: Implement Methods
steps.detail: Add methods for common operations such as append, delete, and traverse.

steps.title: Test the Linked List
steps.detail: Create an instance of the linked list and call the methods to ensure they work as expected.

faqs.question: What are the advantages of using a linked list?
faqs.answer: Linked lists allow for dynamic memory allocation and efficient insertions/deletions compared to arrays.

faqs.question: How does a linked list differ from an array?
faqs.answer: Unlike arrays, linked lists do not require contiguous memory and can grow or shrink in size dynamically.

faqs.question: Can I implement a linked list in any programming language?
faqs.answer: Yes, linked lists can be implemented in most programming languages that support object-oriented or structured programming.

caveats: Linked lists have higher memory overhead due to storing pointers.
Accessing elements is slower compared to arrays due to non-contiguous memory allocation.
